seoTitle: Detroit Uber & Lyft Accident Lawyer: Which Policy Pays, the $1 Million Coverage, and Who Pays a Passenger’s Bills
seoDescription: Hurt in an Uber or Lyft crash in Detroit, as a passenger, a driver, or in another car? Michigan law sets the rideshare insurance by what the app was doing: $1 million on a trip, state minimums while waiting, nothing when off. ATLAW’s Dearborn rideshare accident lawyers explain the three periods, who pays no-fault benefits, and how to get the app data. Free review. (313) 406-7606.
tagline: The policy that pays a Detroit rideshare crash depends on one fact: what the app was doing at the moment of impact. Uber and Lyft hold that record. The first step is a letter demanding they keep it.
primaryKeyword: detroit uber accident lawyer (30/mo) · detroit lyft accident lawyer (30/mo)

c.v: An Uber or Lyft crash in Detroit is a Michigan no-fault car crash with one added question that decides what the claim is worth: what was the app doing at the moment of impact? If a ride had been accepted or a passenger was on board, a $1 million policy applies. If the driver was logged in and waiting, only the Act’s minimum limits apply, $50,000 per person and $100,000 per accident (MCL 257.2123(2)). If the app was off, the driver’s personal policy applies, and that policy may exclude rideshare driving altogether. Uber and Lyft hold the record that answers the question, and they do not volunteer it. Everything else about the case, who pays your medical bills, whether the company itself can be sued, how a Detroit court handles the arbitration clause in the app’s terms, follows from that first answer.

sections.heading: The three periods, and how to prove which one applied

c.v: Michigan regulates Uber, Lyft, and similar companies as transportation network companies under 2016 PA 345, MCL 257.2101 and following. The Act requires insurance in three periods (MCL 257.2123):

rows.v: Driver’s insurer, which may exclude rideshare use
Logged in, waiting for a request
$50,000 per person / $100,000 per crash / $25,000 property damage, plus PIP and PPI
Uber or Lyft, or the driver’s rideshare endorsement
Ride accepted or passenger on board
En route to pick up, or carrying a passenger

c.v: The moment the driver accepts a ride, the $1 million policy attaches and stays attached until the passenger is dropped off. The gap period, app on with no ride, has coverage only at Michigan’s minimums, which is why a serious injury in that period usually turns on the injured person’s own uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage.
Proving the period.
Uber and Lyft keep trip logs, GPS traces, and timestamps for every driver session. A
preservation letter

to the company and its insurer in the first days, followed by a subpoena if necessary, obtains them. A driver who says “I was off the app” is confirmed or contradicted by the record. Screenshot the trip screen, the driver’s name and photo, the plate, the route, and the time before you leave the scene, if you can; it is the one piece of evidence the companies will not preserve for you.
firm’s practice of sending the preservation request in the first days
If you were a passenger.

Michigan no-fault pays your medical expenses and wage loss regardless of fault, but being a paying customer does not put Uber’s insurer first in line. In general, your own auto policy pays first, or a policy held by your spouse or a relative you live with; if there is none, you claim through the Michigan Assigned Claims Plan (MCL 500.3114, as amended by 2016 PA 345; MCL 500.3172).
PIP priority order for a TNC passenger, carried from the rideshare hub

In Detroit, where many passengers have no auto policy and no insured household member, the rideshare policy’s PIP is reached more often than in the suburbs, and the Assigned Claims Plan after it. Written notice to the responsible insurer is due within one year (MCL 500.3145(1)); see our
no-fault insurance claim page
If you were the rideshare driver.

Your own policy pays PIP if it does not exclude rideshare use; if it does, the company’s policy covers PIP while the app is on. Drivers are generally independent contractors under the Act, so there is usually no workers' compensation claim, which makes the PIP claim and the claim against the at-fault driver everything. A personal policy can be rescinded if rideshare use was misrepresented when the policy was bought, which leaves the driver effectively uninsured for personal driving as well; read your policy before the crash, not after.
If you were in another car, on a bike, or on foot.

Your own no-fault insurer pays your benefits, as in any crash (or the priority chain under MCL 500.3114 and 3115 for pedestrians and cyclists). The rideshare period decides which liability policy you claim against for pain and suffering. See our

c.v: uninsured motorist page
Uber or Lyft directly

items.v: , in limited circumstances. Because drivers are generally independent contractors (MCL 257.2137), the companies are not automatically liable for a driver’s negligence. They can be liable for their own: approving a driver who failed, or should have failed, the criminal and driving-record checks the Act requires before approval and annually after (MCL 257.2107); keeping a driver on the platform after impairment complaints, which the Act requires them to suspend pending investigation (MCL 257.2139); or allowing a vehicle that failed the required inspection (MCL 257.2109). These claims are contested and fact-specific.

c.v: The arbitration clause.

items.v: Uber’s and Lyft’s terms of service require passengers to arbitrate disputes with the company. Courts have generally enforced those clauses against claims brought against the companies themselves; they do not bind your claim against the driver’s insurer or the other driver, which proceed in the Third Judicial Circuit Court like any Detroit injury suit.

c.v: current enforceability and scope
Downtown and the venues.

Ford Field, Comerica Park, Little Caesars Arena, the Fox, the casinos, and Huntington Place generate surges of rideshare pickups in a few blocks of Woodward, Brush, and Montcalm at the same minute. The crashes are low-speed sideswipes, rear-ends, pedestrian strikes at pickup curbs, and door strikes of cyclists.
The bar districts after midnight.

Greektown, Corktown, Midtown, and Eastern Market. The rideshare driver is sober by rule (the Act imposes zero tolerance while logged on, MCL 257.2139); the drivers around them often are not. Wayne County recorded 1,331 alcohol-involved crashes in 2024. A bar that over-served the driver who hit the Uber can be liable under the dram shop act (MCL 436.1801), with a 120-day notice. See our
drunk driving accident page

I-94 from downtown through Dearborn to the Merriman Road exit for Detroit Metropolitan Airport, at freeway speed, often with luggage and multiple passengers. These are the serious-injury rideshare cases, often involving
brain
and

injuries, and the $1 million policy is usually in force. Rideshare crashes elsewhere in the county follow the same rules; see our
Wayne County page
The freeways and arterials.
I-75, I-96, the Lodge, Gratiot, Grand River, Michigan Avenue, and Jefferson, where the rideshare driver is one of many and the question is often whether the other driver was insured. See our
Detroit car accident page
for the roads and the intersections.
Windsor passengers.

Trips to and from the tunnel and bridge carry Ontario residents, whose own coverage is under a different system and who generally have no Michigan PIP claim if their vehicle was not insured in Michigan (MCL 500.3113(c)); as rideshare passengers they claim through the chain above.

faqs.question: I was a passenger in an Uber that crashed in Detroit. Who pays my medical bills?

answer.v: Your own auto insurer first, or a policy held by your spouse or a relative you live with; if there is none, the Assigned Claims Plan. Being a paying passenger does not put Uber’s insurer first for your medical bills; it does make the $1 million policy available for your injury claim.

faqs.question: Does Uber or Lyft have to carry insurance in Michigan?

answer.v: Yes: $1 million while a ride is accepted or a passenger is on board; $50,000 / $100,000 / $25,000 while the app is on with no ride; nothing while the app is off, when the driver’s personal policy applies.

faqs.question: An Uber hit my car on Gratiot. Who do I claim against?

answer.v: The policy that applied in that period. If a passenger was on board or a ride was accepted, the $1 million policy. The driver is generally an independent contractor, so Uber itself is usually liable only for its own negligence.

faqs.question: I drive for Lyft in Detroit and was hit by an uninsured driver while waiting for a ride. What now?

answer.v: Your no-fault benefits come from your own policy (or the company’s if yours excludes rideshare use). Your injury claim is a UM claim under whatever UM coverage applies in the waiting period; the Act does not require Uber or Lyft to carry UM, so your own policy’s UM coverage is what matters.

faqs.question: Can I sue Uber or Lyft directly?

answer.v: Only for the company’s own negligence, such as approving a driver who should have failed the background check or keeping one on after impairment complaints. The arbitration clause in the app’s terms may send that claim to arbitration; your claim against the driver’s insurer is not affected.

faqs.question: How do I prove the driver was on a trip?

answer.v: Uber and Lyft keep trip and GPS logs. A preservation letter, and a subpoena if needed, obtains them. Your own screenshots from the scene are the backup.

faqs.question: The driver says the app was off. Does that end my claim?

answer.v: No. The company’s records decide it, not the driver’s statement. And if the app was off, the driver’s personal policy applies; if that policy excludes rideshare use, the exclusion must be read against what the driver was actually doing.
One year to notify the responsible no-fault insurer, three years to sue, and as little as 120 days for a dram shop notice. The app data should be requested within days.
